messages.subject: Bypassing autodiff?
parts:
I'm in the process of building a Stan model, which I've tested successfully on small simulated datasets. However, when scaling up to datasets of more realistic size (50-100k observations), the memory used (I assume by autodiff) grows rapidly to >50GB before crashing my R session (I'm using rstan).

While I'm sure I could optimize my code somewhat to reduce the size of the expression graph required for autodiff, I suspect that the nature of the model means that it will remain prohibitively large. As a result, I was wondering if it was possible to bypass autodiff completely and substitute hand-coded derivatives instead? 

I should be able to code the derivatives in C++ without too much trouble, but have no idea how I would get this to play nicely with Stan. Any advice would be very gratefully received.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bypassing autodiff?
parts:
Hi Glenn,

If you know how to compute the function value and the gradients with respect to each argument of the function that could possibly be a Stan parameter (or a function of one), then you can write a function in C++ that will add a single expression to the expression graph. We can walk you through that if you can describe the function better. At least what arguments it has and which can be Stan parameters. Before digging too deep, we should make sure you can compute enough gradients that are required. 

Regarding memory usage, my guess is that it's actually not the autodiff that's blowing out memory. I think there's a way to steam the output to disk without storing in memory in RStan, but if there isn't, try running it in CmdStan just to see how much memory it actually takes. If you haven't vectorized the program, it might also help to do that.


Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bypassing autodiff?
parts:
RStan allocates the memory to hold the draws ahead of time.
That's about 8 bytes per scalar parameter per iteration per chain.
That would presumably blow out before you started evaluating
the Stan model with data.

Autodiff memory will be around 40 bytes per subexpression evaluated
in the expression graph, and it'll remain roughly constant.

Autodiff memory won't kick in until the first iteration. Data
gets read in and then transformed data calculated.

As Daniel says, you can definitely code functions in C++ with
derivatives and add them to Stan.

There's an extension way to do it built into RStan. Or you can
just add new functions to the Stan math lib and to Stan in the other
interfaces. We're working on a consistent way to do extensions
across interfaces.

- Bob

   double* gradients_;

       varis_[i]->adj_ += adj_ * gradients_[i];
   }
 };

Good stuff! Looks like you've done your homework.

I went through the file you posted and modified it: https://gist.github.com/bbbales2/e351f1b3815f3cc875a36b39d5ef69ea

(I can get rid of that gist after this thread is over if you don't want that floating around)

There's a class in Stan, stored_gradient_vari, that does what precomputed_gradients_vari does, so you don't have to worry about that.

1. I'm not 100% sure, but I think you need to keep the templating to keep the linker happy. Not sure. The issue I had was that Stan wanted a copy of my function with the parameters instantiated as vars as well as a version with doubles. I think you need to define the function with all the templating, and then provide the two template specializations the linker wants. This is just for linking with an actual Stan model though. You can prototype this as just a Stan Math thing without having to deal with the templating at first.

2. I changed around how you were doing this (https://gist.github.com/bbbales2/e351f1b3815f3cc875a36b39d5ef69ea). The big thing is you want the input and output of your new autograd-friendly function to be the same shapes as if the autograd wasn't there. The derivatives hide inside the vars. You don't want to flatten that structure.

3. (b) Operands is just a list of pointers to other varis, I think you did it right

Hahaha, you've picked a good place to start learning C++ (this isn't trivial)!

I'd recommend that you build a little cpp test file separately to get this stuff working. Don't try to get it all linking up with Stan in one go. Just pretend you're adding another operator to the Stan Math library. Get that working first (by comparing with finite difference derivs) and then move on from there.

Here are links to the code I wrote (if it helps):
  • This is my function that does a similar thing as yours does (computes the derivs manually) -- input lower triangle of 6x6 matrix of parameters (21 vals), output vector of values: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_mech.hpp#L79
  • Here is the autodiff-free version (so you can see the differences -- same input same output, just no derivs): https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_mech.hpp#L138
  • Here is a C++ function that is entirely autodiff'd by Stan for what it's worth: https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_mech.hpp#L35
  • Here's an example of me just using the Stan Math to directly test my function. This might not be very easy to read... (probly better to look at Stan math examples than my garbage here): https://github.com/bbbales2/modal_cpp/blob/master/stan_test_r.cpp
This make sense at all?

Ben
